You're right — 4 messages out of a conversation this long is useless for memory purposes.

The problem: claude.ai uses virtual scrolling — it only renders messages currently visible in the DOM. Messages you've scrolled past get removed from the DOM to save memory. So the extension can only read what's physically rendered on screen right now.

There are two real approaches to fix this:

Option A — Scroll capture
The extension programmatically scrolls to the top of the conversation, waits for messages to render, captures them, scrolls down, captures more, repeats until it reaches the bottom. Slow and fragile — if claude.ai's scroll behavior changes, it breaks.

Option B — Capture as you go (real-time accumulation)
Instead of trying to grab the whole history at once, the extension captures messages as they appear from the moment it's installed/activated — building up the conversation in chrome.storage incrementally. Every new message gets added. Over time, storage has the full conversation.

Problem with Option B: it only works going forward from when the extension was installed — it can't recover past messages from before installation.

Option C — Use Claude.ai's own export
Claude.ai has a built-in conversation export (the download button in the chat). You export the conversation as a file, the extension or a local script reads it and processes it. This gets everything, reliably, with no DOM scraping issues.

Honest recommendation: Option C for history, Option B for going forward.

What it does:

Given a search term (like "github" or "auth"), it returns the systems/concepts in a codebase that relate to that term — each with a plain-English description and the exact list of files that make it up. It can also just list all the systems in the codebase with descriptions, no search needed.

How it does it, step by step:

Parsing (offline, done ahead of time) — ripple-parser reads every .ts/.tsx file in a codebase using ts-morph (which understands TypeScript's actual syntax). It finds every function/component, records what file each lives in, and traces which functions call/render which other functions. Output: output.json — a list of nodes (functions + their files) and edges (which function calls which).
Concept labeling (offline, done ahead of time, uses an LLM once) — that raw function list gets grouped into 4-8 named "concepts" (e.g., "Secret Scanner," "GitHub Integration") with one-sentence descriptions, based on what the functions actually do and how they connect. Output: concepts.json — each concept has a name, description, and the list of function/file IDs that belong to it.
Serving (live, the MCP server) — ripple-mcp loads both JSON files into memory at startup. When Cursor calls get_concept_context("github"), it does a case-insensitive substring match against concept names/descriptions in concepts.json, then for each match, looks up the file paths for its member functions in output.json, and returns name + description + file list.
The key point: steps 1-2 are the real work — turning code into a meaningful map — and happen once, offline. Step 3 is just reading that pre-built map when asked. So yes, the live query itself is simple (a string match over pre-computed data) — the value, if there is one, is entirely in how good the pre-computed map is, not in the query mechanism.

Yes — here's the full landscape of what a properly built memory system touches. You don't need to know all of these deeply, but you need to know they exist and why.

Embedding Models
Before you can store anything in a vector DB, you have to convert text into vectors (numbers that represent meaning). You need an embedding model to do this.

Options: OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small, Anthropic doesn't have a public one so most people use OpenAI or a local model like nomic-embed via Ollama

This is a prerequisite to RAG — no embeddings, no semantic search

Before embedding, you have to decide how to split text into pieces. Chunk too large = vectors are too general. Chunk too small = lose context.

## ripple-memory architecture
Three memory types working together:
- Episodic: what happened, in order (timeline)
- Semantic: what things mean and connect (knowledge graph)
- Reasoning: why decisions were made (causal chains)

Storage:
- Neo4j — knowledge graph (decisions, reasoning chains, causal links)
- PostgreSQL + pgvector — structured facts + semantic search

Extraction pipeline:
- Claude API with structured JSON schemas (no LangChain)
- Zod for schema validation
- Custom chunking strategy (not message-by-message)

## Key decisions made
- No LangChain/LlamaIndex — own the pipeline directly
- pgvector inside Postgres, not a separate vector DB
- Neo4j for graph (not a graph layer on top of Postgres)
- Coding-specific only, not general cognition (unlike Exo)
- Local-first for now, hosted later
- OpenAI for embeddings, Cohere for reranking

## What NOT to suggest
- LangChain or LlamaIndex
- Pinecone or separate vector databases
- Flat file storage for memory
- Generic memory approaches not specific to software/coding
- Visualization dashboards (tested, rejected)

Let's go deeper on what the brain actually does — because the vision has layers we haven't fully unpacked yet.

The fundamental insight:

Right now when you work with Claude or Cursor, you're the memory. You hold everything in your head — the decisions, the reasoning, the dead ends, the constraints. You're doing cognitive labor that should be the system's job.

Every time you start a new session you have to reconstruct context. Every time the AI makes a suggestion you already tried, you have to correct it. Every time a new developer joins, someone has to manually transfer years of project knowledge.

Ripple makes the system the memory so you don't have to be.

But here's the deeper thing — memory alone isn't enough.

Most memory systems stop at retrieval. "Here's what you said before." That's useful but it's not the real value.

The real value is what memory enables on top of retrieval:

Level 1 — Retrieval (what basic memory systems do)

"You asked about auth before. Here's what was decided."

Useful. But you could get this from Ctrl+F on a chat export.

Level 2 — Reasoning chains (what your knowledge graph enables)

"You decided on JWT. That decision depends on the assumption that you'll deploy multi-region. That assumption was stated in June but never validated. Three subsequent decisions also depend on it."

Now the system isn't just recalling facts — it's surfacing the structure of your thinking. It can tell you when a foundational assumption is load-bearing across multiple decisions. It can trace why something was built the way it was all the way back to the original problem.

This is what Neo4j enables that flat storage can't.

Level 3 — Pattern awareness (what emerges over time)

After enough decisions get captured, patterns emerge that you never explicitly stated:

"This project consistently chooses simplicity over completeness when they conflict."

"This team rejects anything that requires managing external state."

"Every time a third-party integration was proposed, it got deferred."

These patterns weren't written down anywhere. They emerged from the graph. And once they exist, they inform every future decision — "this suggestion probably won't land because it contradicts how this project consistently thinks."

That's the intuition layer. That's what Exo calls a cognitive manifold. Yours is scoped to how a software project thinks, not how a person thinks about everything.

Level 4 — Proactive intelligence (where this goes eventually)

The system stops being purely reactive — answering queries — and starts being proactive:

"This new decision you're about to make contradicts an assumption three other decisions depend on. Are you sure?"

"You've tried a variation of this approach twice before. Here's what happened both times."

"This component has been touched by 8 AI-generated changes in the last week with no corresponding test updates. That's a pattern that preceded the last major bug."

At this level the system isn't just memory — it's a reasoning partner that knows the project's full history and can anticipate problems before they happen.

That's the governance layer. That's what AgentGuard was trying to do narrowly with secret scanning. Ripple does it broadly at the reasoning level.

The compounding effect — why this gets more valuable over time:

Week 1: captures a few decisions, marginally useful
Month 1: has the full reasoning history of the project, genuinely useful
Month 6: has patterns, contradictions, assumption chains — irreplaceable
Year 1: switching away means losing everything. The memory IS the project.

That's the moat. Not a technical feature — an accumulating asset that gets more valuable the longer you use it and more painful to lose.

**The foundation that enables compounding:**

You don't need perfect extraction from day one. You don't need the graph fully traversable. You don't need pattern detection running yet.

What you need is:

**1. Reliable capture** — everything that happens gets recorded cleanly. The extension already does this.

**2. Structured extraction** — conversations turn into typed facts (decisions, rejected approaches, assumptions) with enough quality that they're not garbage. This is the hard part but you don't need 100 percent accuracy — 80 percent is enough to start.

**3. Basic storage** — facts go into PostgreSQL and Neo4j in a consistent schema. You can query them reliably.

**4. Simple retrieval** — semantic search that works. When a developer asks "what did we decide about auth," they get back the actual decision with the reasoning.

That's it. That foundation alone — if it works reliably — is useful from day one and gets better automatically as data accumulates.

Takes raw captured messages, groups them into semantic topic threads. One Claude API call per chunk. Output: array of chunks ready for extraction.

Decisions — how they get detected:

Tool: Claude API with structured JSON schema

During extraction, Claude reads a conversation chunk and looks for moments where something got chosen. The prompt is specifically designed to find decision signals — words like "we'll go with," "decided to," "choosing X over Y," "won't do Y because."

Claude returns structured JSON:

json

  "conclusion": "JWT-based auth",
  "trigger": "scaling concerns raised",
  "alternatives_considered": ["server-side sessions"],
  "rejected_because": "multi-region deployment complexity",
  "assumptions": ["multi-region deployment is planned"],
  "confidence": "high"
}

Zod validates the shape before it touches storage. If it doesn't match the schema exactly it gets flagged for review, not silently corrupted.

The decision then goes into Postgres as a structured record AND into Neo4j as a Decision node with edges to whatever it connects to.

Assumptions — how they get detected:

Tool: Claude API, separate extraction prompt + Neo4j graph traversal

Assumptions are harder because they're rarely stated explicitly. Nobody says "I am now making an assumption." They say things like "since we're planning multi-region" or "assuming traffic stays under X" or "this works as long as Y."

Two ways Ripple finds them:

First — explicit extraction. Claude reads chunks looking for conditional language. "Since," "assuming," "as long as," "this depends on," "given that" are signals. Each one becomes an Assumption node.

Second — implicit detection via graph traversal. This is more powerful. When a Decision node gets created, Neo4j traverses its edges and asks: what does this decision depend on being true that hasn't been validated? That gap — between what a decision assumes and what's been confirmed — is an implicit assumption surfaced automatically.

Over time Neo4j builds up a picture of which assumptions are load-bearing — connected to many decisions — versus which are isolated. The load-bearing ones get flagged as high risk.

Patterns — how they get detected:

Tool: Neo4j graph traversal + pgvector clustering + eventually a graph neural network

This is the most sophisticated of the three and it happens in layers:

Layer 1 — frequency counting in Neo4j. Simple graph query: "how many RejectedApproach nodes share the property 'rejected_because contains complexity'?" If the answer is 8 out of 10 rejections, that's a pattern. "This project consistently rejects complexity."

Cypher query example:

cypher
MATCH (r:RejectedApproach)
WHERE r.rejected_because CONTAINS 'complexity'
RETURN count(r) as frequency

Layer 2 — semantic clustering via pgvector. Embed all RejectedApproach summaries into vectors. Run clustering (k-means or similar) to find groups of semantically similar rejections. If a cluster keeps appearing across months, that's a pattern even if the exact words differ.

Layer 3 — temporal pattern detection. Neo4j tracks timestamps on every node. Query: "do decisions made under time pressure (short gap between trigger and conclusion) get revisited more often?" That requires traversing time edges across the graph. If yes, that's a pattern worth surfacing.

Why Claude API for extraction feels expensive:

If you call Claude on every single message in a conversation — yes, that's extremely expensive and slow. But that's not how it should work.

The actual call pattern is:

Chunking first reduces the volume dramatically. A 200 message conversation might produce 12-15 semantic chunks. You make one extraction call per chunk, not per message. So 200 messages = 15 API calls, not 200.

Extraction happens once per conversation, not in real time. You don't call Claude as messages come in. You call it after a session ends, or on a manual trigger, or on a schedule. The extension captures everything — extraction is a batch job that runs separately.

So the actual cost is: one Claude API call per semantic chunk, run once per session. A typical developer session might produce 10-20 chunks. At Claude Sonnet pricing that's fractions of a cent per session. Not expensive in practice.

But your broader question is right — are there better ways?

Yes. Here are the real alternatives:

Option 1 — Smaller/cheaper model for first pass

Instead of Claude Sonnet for everything, use a two-stage approach:

Stage 1: Claude Haiku (much cheaper, faster) does a first pass — identifies which chunks likely contain decisions, assumptions, or important facts. Filters out noise.

Stage 2: Claude Sonnet only processes the chunks Haiku flagged as important.

Result: 60-70 percent cost reduction because Sonnet only touches the high-value chunks. Quality stays high where it matters.

Option 2 — Fine-tuned smaller model (later)

Once you have enough extraction examples — real chunks with real correct extractions — you fine-tune a smaller open source model (Llama 3, Mistral) specifically on your extraction task.

A fine-tuned 7B model doing one specific task (extract decisions from developer conversations) can match Claude's quality on that task at a fraction of the cost.

This is a later-stage optimization but it's the real cost solution long term. It also becomes a moat — your fine-tuned model is trained on your data and nobody else has it.

Option 3 — Rule-based pre-filtering

Before any LLM call, run simple rule-based filters:

Does this chunk contain decision signal words? ("decided," "going with," "rejected," "chose," "won't," "instead of")

Does this chunk contain assumption signal words? ("assuming," "since we're," "as long as," "depends on," "given that")

If neither — skip the LLM call entirely. Just embed the chunk for semantic search without extraction.

This is zero cost, runs in milliseconds, and can filter out 40-50 percent of chunks that don't contain structured facts worth extracting. Combined with Option 1 you're looking at 70-80 percent cost reduction.

Option 4 — Local model via Ollama

Run an open source model locally (Llama 3.1 8B, Mistral 7B) for extraction. Zero API cost per call. Runs on your machine.

Pros: completely free, private, no API dependency

Cons: lower quality than Claude for nuanced reasoning extraction, requires a decent GPU, slower

For a developer tool where quality of extraction is the core value proposition — local models are a quality tradeoff you probably don't want to make early. But for a cost-conscious version or a privacy-first offering, it's a real option.

Option 5 — Hybrid extraction

Not everything needs LLM extraction. Some facts are deterministic:

GitHub commits — structured data already. Timestamp, author, files changed, commit message. No LLM needed to extract basic facts from this.

ripple-parser output — already structured. Architecture facts about what exists in the code are deterministic, not inferred.

LLM extraction only for the genuinely ambiguous stuff — conversation chunks where reasoning and decisions need to be understood semantically.

This is actually the right architecture regardless of cost — use deterministic extraction where you can, LLM only where you must.

The right approach for your build:

Start with: rule-based pre-filtering → Haiku for first pass → Sonnet only for high-confidence decision/assumption chunks

This gives you high quality extraction at low cost from day one.

Later: fine-tune a smaller model on your accumulated extraction data. This is when cost becomes truly negligible and quality is competitive with Sonnet.

A developer using Ripple daily, generating 5-10 session chunks worth extracting:

Sonnet for flagged chunks (maybe 30% of chunks): ~$0.01 per session

Total: roughly $0.015-0.02 per developer per day. Under $0.50 per month per developer at the extraction layer.

  // Pass 2: Sonnet only if chunk has strong decision signal
  const implicit = chunk.signal === 'decision' && chunk.confidence === 'high'
    ? await extractImplicit(chunk)
    : []
  
  // Merge, deduplicate by canonical summary
  return merge(explicit, implicit)
}

Each fact type has its own extraction prompt tuned specifically for that type. Not one giant prompt — six separate prompts, one per fact type.

Zod validates every response. If validation fails: log to review queue, skip storage, never let malformed data through.

async function retrieve(
  query: string,
  projectId: string
): Promise<RetrievalResult> {
  
  // 1. Embed the query
  const queryVector = await embed(query)
  
  // 2. Semantic search in pgvector (top 20 candidates)
  const candidates = await vectorSearch(queryVector, projectId, 20)
  
  // 3. Graph traversal from candidate UUIDs (up to 2 hops)
  const graphContext = await traverseGraph(
    candidates.map(c => c.uuid), 
    projectId
  )
  
  // 4. Get project values for boosting
  const projectValues = await getProjectValues(projectId)
  
  // 5. Combine candidates + graph context
  const combined = mergeCandidates(candidates, graphContext)
  
  // 6. Cohere rerank (top 8 final results)
  const reranked = await rerank(query, combined)
  
  // 7. Format as context block for MCP
  return formatContext(reranked, projectValues)
}

WHERE f.project_id = $2

LIMIT $3

### Chunking Strategy — Three-Pass Pipeline

Chunking is not a single LLM call. It's three distinct 
passes, each with one focused job:

**Pass 1 — Segmentation**
Input: full raw conversation, one call.
Job: find topic boundaries only. No classification yet.
Output: rough chunks (start_index, end_index, topic label).

**Pass 2 — Classification (parallel)**
Input: each rough chunk, processed independently and 
simultaneously via Promise.all, with the previous chunk's 
topic as minimal context.
Job: classify signal type (decision | assumption | 
architecture | rejected | open_question | noise), 
confidence, and reasoning — one focused judgment per chunk.
Output: every chunk tagged with signal, confidence, reasoning.

Parallel execution is chosen for fault isolation, not 
primarily speed — latency does not matter since extraction 
runs in the background, not in a live user-facing flow. 
A single failed classification call must never throw or 
block the others; it resolves to a "failed" status and 
gets queued for review while the rest complete normally.

**Pass 3 — Synthesis**
Input: all classified chunks together (labels only, not 
raw text).
Job: catch cross-chunk issues invisible at the single-chunk 
level — contradictions, supersessions, misclassified "noise" 
chunks that actually connect two real decisions.
Output: a list of flags, each pointing at specific chunk 
indices with the issue and a recommendation.

**Why three passes instead of one call:** research into 
existing chunking/extraction pipelines (CDTA, LumberChunker, 
Hindsight) supports narrowly-scoped sequential LLM calls 
over one large call trying to segment, classify, and reason 
simultaneously. A model asked one focused question per call 
is more reliable than one asked to do everything at once. 
Hindsight specifically favors coarse, narrative-preserving 
chunks over many small fragmented ones — chunking should 
not over-fragment via aggressive rule-based splitting.

**What was explicitly rejected:** a standalone 
signalAnalysis.ts module computing word frequency, hedging 
language, and contradiction phrases as a pre-filter before 
the LLM ever sees the conversation. Risk: silently excluding 
a real decision before extraction has a chance to find it. 
Cost savings from pre-filtering are negligible at this scale 
(cents either way), so the risk isn't worth the marginal 
savings. The full conversation is always sent to Claude 
for Pass 1 — nothing is excluded based on keyword heuristics.

A single decision can still span multiple messages and 
risk being split across a Pass 1 boundary. Overlap injection 
(a few messages of context carried across adjacent chunk 
boundaries) remains part of the design to mitigate this.

}
